2 Novel THE LOST WORLD

CHAPTER
A Dream of Adventure
Novel THE LOST WORLD 3

A Dream of Adventure
My name is Edward Malone, and at the time this story began I was a young reporter
on the Daily Gazette in London. I was twenty-three, full of energy, and certain that
a great life was waiting for me. The problem was that I had no idea how to begin it.
There was also Gladys Hungerton. I admired her more than anyone I had ever met,
and one evening I finally asked her to marry me. She did not laugh at me or become
angry. Instead, she looked serious and told me that she valued our friendship but
did not love me in the way I hoped.
Gladys said "I love a man who has done something brave. Someone who has faced
danger, traveled into the unknown, and proved that he can act when it matters."
I tried to joke. "So I must discover a new country before you will consider me?"
"Not for me," she replied. "If a man is truly brave, he does not act just to impress
someone else. He acts because courage is part of his character."
Her words stayed with me. I left her house feeling disappointed, but also strangely
excited.
London suddenly seemed too safe. I wanted a challenge - something that would test
me and give my life a clearer purpose.
The next evening I went straight to my editor, Mr McArdle. He was an experienced
newspaper man who had seen every kind of young reporter. When I asked him to
send me on a dangerous assignment, he pushed his glasses up and stared at me.
"You want danger?" he said. "Most sensible people want to avoid it." "I want a real
story, sir. Something difficult."
He studied me for a moment, then smiled. "Perhaps I do have a job for you. Have
you heard of Professor George Edward Challenger?"
Of course I had. Almost everyone in the newspaper world knew his name.
Challenger was a famous zoologist, brilliant but extremely difficult. He had
recently returned from South America with an extraordinary story about unknown
4 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: animals. When scientists questioned him, he refused to give clear details. When
pages.text:
animals. When scientists questioned him, he refused to give clear details. When
reporters tried to interview him, he often threw them out of his house - sometimes
literally.
"Do you want me to interview him?" I asked.
"If you can get through the front door," McArdle replied. "Two years ago
Challenger traveled alone through a little-known part of South America. He
came back claiming that something remarkable had happened. He had damaged
photographs, strange sketches, and a few pieces
of evidence, but he would not reveal the exact place. Most people think he is either
mistaken or lying. Find out which."
This was exactly the kind of chance I had been looking for. Yet there was one
problem: Challenger hated journalists. If I arrived honestly and said I worked for
the Gazette, the interview would probably end before it began.
That night I went to the Savage Club, where many writers and scientists met. I
found my friend Tarp Henry, who worked for a scientific journal, and asked what
he knew about Challenger.
"He is clever," Henry said, "but impossible. He argues with everyone. At a
scientific meeting in Vienna he almost started a battle over a theory of evolution. If
you want to speak to him, do not mention newspapers."
That gave me an idea. I asked Henry to find Challenger's latest scientific paper. It
was full of technical language I barely understood, but I copied one complicated
sentence and used it in a letter. I pretended to be a young student who admired
Challenger's work but had a question about one of his arguments.
Henry read the letter and laughed. "You are taking a risk, Malone. He may realize
at once that you know nothing about the subject."
"I only need to get inside his study," I said. "After that, I will take my chance."
Two days later a reply arrived. The handwriting looked as aggressive as the man
himself. Challenger wrote that my question showed poor understanding, but he was
Novel THE LOST WORLD 5

pages.topic: willing to explain the matter in person. He gave me an appointment for eleven
pages.text:
willing to explain the matter in person. He gave me an appointment for eleven
o'clock on Wednesday morning.
I should have been nervous. Instead, I felt as if my real life had finally begun.
On Wednesday I traveled to Professor Challenger's large house in Kensington. A
quiet servant named Austin opened the door. Before he could take me to the study,
a small, lively woman stopped me in the hall.
"You have come to see my husband?" she asked. "Yes, Mrs Challenger."
She lowered her voice. "Then I should warn you. George is a perfectly impossible
person. If he becomes angry, do not argue too long."
A deep voice suddenly roared from behind a closed door. Austin opened it, and I
entered. Professor Challenger sat behind
a wide desk covered with books, maps,
fossils, and papers.
He was shorter than I expected, but
enormously broad. His black beard
spread across his chest, and his sharp
grey-blue eyes seemed to measure every
weakness in me.
"Well?" he demanded. "You are
the young man who has difficulty
understanding plain science?"
I had entered looking for adventure. I had
found it sooner than I expected.
Chapter Summative
6 Novel THE LOST WORLD

CHAPTER
Professor Challenger's Secret
Novel THE LOST WORLD 9

Professor Challenger's Secret
Professor Challenger began by asking me questions
about the scientific article I had mentioned in my letter.
At first I tried to answer confidently, but the questions
became more technical every minute.
"And what do you think of the recent evidence?" he
asked. "Very interesting," I said carefully.
"Which evidence?" I hesitated.
His eyes narrowed. "You know nothing about this
subject."
There was no point pretending any longer. "Very little,
" I admitted. "Then why are you here?"
I took a breath. "I am a reporter for the Daily Gazette."
For one silent second, nothing happened. Then
Challenger rose from his chair like a storm. "A journalist!
In my house!"
He came towards me. I told him firmly not to touch
me. He ignored the warning. A moment later we were
struggling in the hallway, crashing into a chair and
rolling through the open front door. We landed together
on the steps outside.
A policeman hurried over. Several neighbors stopped to
watch. "What happened?" the policeman asked.
My eye was beginning to swell, and Challenger's coat
was torn. I could easily have made a complaint. Instead,
I remembered that I had entered his house under a false
name and had deliberately tricked him.
"It was partly my fault," I said. "I will not press charges."
The policeman looked surprised, but closed his notebook.
Challenger stared at me. The anger in his face changed
into something almost like respect.
10 Novel THE LOST WORLD

"Come back inside," he said.
I followed him, wondering whether I was brave or simply foolish.
Back in the study, Challenger closed the door and became suddenly serious.
"You behaved better than I would expect from a reporter," he said. "Perhaps I
will show you something. But you must promise not to publish it without my
permission."
I gave him my word.
He opened a worn sketchbook. "Two years ago I traveled through the Amazon
region to study animal life. In a remote village I found a dying American named
Maple White. He had reached the village alone after terrible hardship. He died
before I could question him."
Among White's belongings, Challenger had found the sketchbook. Most of the
early pages showed ordinary river scenes, plants, people, and animals. Then the
drawings changed.
One picture showed a line of high red cliffs rising above thick forest. The cliffs
seemed to form an enormous natural wall. Another showed a separate rock tower
standing near them. On top was a tree.
"A strange landscape," I said, "but hardly impossible." "Continue."
The next drawing stopped me. It showed a huge animal with a heavy body, long
tail, and plates rising along its back.
"What is that?"
"That," said Challenger, "is the question. Maple White drew what he saw."
He opened a reference book and showed me an illustration of a prehistoric
stegosaurus.
The similarity was remarkable.
"A man can draw anything," I said.
"Of course. Which is why I went to find the place myself."
Challenger explained that he followed White's route using clues in the sketchbook.
After weeks of travel, he found the red cliffs. He could not climb onto the high
Novel THE LOST WORLD 11

pages.topic: plateau, but he saw extraordinary creatures there. He took photographs, though
pages.text:
plateau, but he saw extraordinary creatures there. He took photographs, though
most were damaged later in a river accident.
He showed me one photograph. The image was unclear, but I could see the cliffs
and the isolated rock tower. On the tree at the top appeared a large dark shape.
"A bird?" I suggested.
Challenger shook his head. "Look more closely."
He handed me a magnifying glass. The creature did have wings, but its outline was
unlike any bird I knew.
Then Challenger opened a drawer and removed a long curved bone with a piece of
dried membrane attached.
"This was part of the creature's wing," he said. "I shot it, but most of the body was
lost in the river accident."
At first I thought it might come from a giant bat. Challenger pointed out the
structure of the bone and compared it with a diagram in a zoology book. Slowly I
understood what he was saying.
"A pterodactyl?" I whispered.
"Exactly. A flying reptile from a
prehistoric age."
I looked again at Maple White's
drawing, the damaged photograph, and
the piece of wing. One item alone might
have been explained away. Together
they were much harder to dismiss.
"You really believe prehistoric animals
are still alive on that plateau?" "I do not
believe," Challenger said proudly. "I
know."
He explained his theory. The plateau
had been cut off from the surrounding world for an extremely long time. Its high
cliffs formed a natural barrier. Plants and animals that disappeared elsewhere might
12 Novel THE LOST WORLD

have survived there in isolation.
"Then why not return with other scientists?" I asked.
His expression darkened. He had tried to speak publicly after returning to London,
but people had accused him of creating false photographs, and demanded exact
directions. Insulted, he had refused to say more.
"Yet truth does not become false because fools refuse to accept it," he said.
For the first time, I saw more than the rude, explosive man described by the
newspapers. Challenger was proud and difficult, but he was also completely certain
of what he had seen. I believed that he believed his story. More than that, I was
beginning to believe it too.
Before I left, he told me about a public lecture at the Zoological Institute the
following evening. A well-known speaker would discuss the history of life on
Earth. Challenger expected his South American claims to be mentioned.
"Attend if you wish," he said. "You may find the evening educational."
As I stepped into the London street, the ordinary traffic seemed suddenly unreal.
Somewhere beyond the Atlantic, perhaps, there was a high red wall of rock where
creatures from millions of years ago still moved through the forest.
I had wanted a great adventure. Now I knew where it might begin.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 13

CHAPTER
The Expedition Is Chosen
16 Novel THE LOST WORLD

The Expedition Is Chosen
The lecture hall of the Zoological Institute was crowded.
Professor Challenger sat near the front, impossible to
miss because of his great black beard and powerful build.
At first the lecture was calm. The speaker described
how life had changed over millions of years. Then he
mentioned stories of prehistoric creatures surviving in
remote regions. There was laughter from part of the
audience.
Challenger stood at once.
“There is nothing amusing about evidence,” he said
loudly.
The chairman asked him to sit down, but the room was
already excited. Professor Summerlee, a thin, elderly
scientist with a sharp face and an even sharper voice,
challenged him directly.
“If Professor Challenger has really found living
prehistoric animals,” Summerlee said, “let him tell us
where they are and provide proof that can be tested.”
Challenger faced him. “Would you be willing to test it
yourself?” The room became silent.
Summerlee lifted his chin. “Yes.”
“Then I will give a properly chosen committee enough
information to reach the place. You may examine it with
your own eyes.”
The audience exploded in cheers and questions.
Challenger raised a hand. “Professor Summerlee should
Novel THE LOST WORLD 17

pages.topic: not travel alone. The journey will be difficult and dangerous. He will require
pages.text:
not travel alone. The journey will be difficult and dangerous. He will require
younger companions. Who volunteers?”
I do not remember deciding to stand. One moment I was seated; the next I was on
my feet. “Edward Malone, Daily Gazette,” I called. “I volunteer.”
Another man stood at almost the same time. He was tall, thin, and sun-browned,
with calm blue eyes.
“Lord John Roxton,” he said. “I know the Amazon country and have traveled there
before.”
Everyone recognized the name. Lord John was famous as an explorer, sportsman,
and hunter. Challenger immediately proposed that Summerlee, Roxton, and I
should form the investigating party.
The motion was accepted. In a few astonishing minutes, my future had changed
completely.
Outside the hall Lord John caught up with me. “So we are to be traveling
companions, Mr Malone. Come to my rooms. We should get to know one another.”
His home was full of maps, books, equipment, and trophies from earlier journeys.
Yet he spoke without showing off. He wanted to know whether I could shoot,
climb, swim, and keep calm under pressure.
“I can learn what I do not know,” I told him.
“Good answer. South America is not a place for a man who thinks he already
knows everything.”
Lord John told me that during one of his earlier journeys, he had become involved
in a serious dispute with a powerful rubber-trading group led by a man named
Pedro Lopez. Local workers were being treated unfairly and forced to work under
terrible conditions. Lord John helped them escape from the group's control and
brought an end to Lopez's influence in the area.
"It made me some loyal friends," he said, "and some dangerous enemies. But I
know the rivers, the language used by many local traders and guides, and the kind
18 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: of men we may need. That could keep us alive."
pages.text:
of men we may need. That could keep us alive."
Over the next weeks we prepared for the expedition. Professor Summerlee
remained openly doubtful about Challenger’s claims, but he was determined to
investigate them properly. I respected his honesty. He might be skeptical, but he
was willing to risk a long journey to discover the truth.
Before we left England, I visited Gladys.
“I am going to South America,” I told her. “There may be real danger.”
For a moment her eyes brightened with interest. “Then you have found your chance.”
I wanted to say that I was doing it for her, but I remembered her earlier words. A
brave act done only to win approval was not true courage. So I simply said, “I hope
I can make good use of it.”
We sailed across the Atlantic and reached Brazil. At Para we hired several men to
help us. The most important was Zambo, a huge, cheerful man who was strong,
loyal, and practical. We also employed two experienced river men, Gomez and
Manuel, and several Indigenous boatmen who knew the upper waterways far better
than any European traveler.
Lord John chose the team carefully. Summerlee spent much of his time studying
insects and plants. I kept notes for the Gazette. Every day the expedition felt more
real.
Our written instructions from Challenger were to be opened at Manaos at exactly
noon on 15 July. The envelope remained sealed during the journey.
At last the day arrived. We sat around a table in a shaded house outside Manaos.
Lord John placed his watch beside the envelope.
“Noon,” he said, and cut it open. Inside was a single sheet of paper. It was blank.
Summerlee stared at it. “This is ridiculous.”
Before anyone could answer, a deep familiar voice came from the doorway. “On
the contrary, Professor Summerlee. It is perfectly sensible.”
Novel THE LOST WORLD 19

pages.topic: Professor Challenger walked into the room.
pages.text:
Professor Challenger walked into the room.
He had secretly traveled to Brazil and planned to guide us himself. No written
directions, he explained, could be as reliable as his own memory. He had kept his
decision private because he did not want arguments, reporters, or curious travelers
following him.
Summerlee looked horrified. “You mean I must spend the whole journey with
you?”
“The scientific value of my company will more than compensate for any personal
discomfort,” Challenger replied.
Lord John laughed. “Then our team is complete.”
Challenger spread a map across the table, though the final destination was not
marked.
“We leave tomorrow,” he said. “From this point onwards, we are going into
a country that very few outsiders have seen. Later we will go beyond even that.”
I looked around the table at the four of us - Challenger, Summerlee, Lord John, and
myself.
We were different in age, character, and purpose. Yet we now shared one question.
Was there truly a lost world waiting beyond the Amazon?
20 Novel THE LOST WORLD

CHAPTER
Into the Unknown
Novel THE LOST WORLD 23

Into the Unknown
Lord John had hired a steam launch called the Esmeralda to carry us up the
Amazon. The river was so wide that, even far inland, the opposite bank often
looked like a distant shadow. Day after day we moved through heat, rain, brilliant
sunlight, and walls of green forest.
Challenger refused to reveal our exact route. He made all of us promise that, even if
we returned safely, we would not publish enough information for strangers to locate
the plateau. He said careless visitors could destroy a place that science had barely
discovered.
After several days we left the main river and entered a large tributary. It gradually
became narrower. At a small riverside village, Challenger ordered the Esmeralda
back to Manaos.
“From here we use canoes,” he said. “Soon there will be rapids. A steam launch
cannot continue.”
We hired two local guides who had accompanied Challenger during his earlier
journey.
They were clearly frightened by the idea of returning, but they knew the route.
For several days our canoes moved through a beautiful green waterway. Monkeys
watched us from branches. Bright birds stood on fallen logs. Once we saw a puma
disappear into the forest. The animals seemed less afraid of humans the farther we
traveled.
Then the water became too shallow. We hid the canoes and continued on foot,
carrying food, rifles, blankets, instruments, and medical supplies.
The land rose steadily. Thick tropical forest gave way to palms, rocky slopes,
orchids, bamboo, and wide areas of tree-ferns. Progress was exhausting. Sometimes
we spent an entire day cutting a path through bamboo so dense that we could see
only a few meters ahead.
Challenger and Summerlee argued constantly.
“We should follow the compass,” Challenger insisted one morning.
24 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: “We should follow the men who have actually walked through this country,”
pages.text:
“We should follow the men who have actually walked through this country,”
Summerlee replied.
Lord John usually prevented the arguments from becoming serious. “Save your
energy, gentlemen. You may need it for something with bigger teeth.”
On the ninth day after leaving the canoes, Challenger suddenly stopped and
pointed.
A huge grey shape rose from the plain ahead. It flapped slowly, flew low across the
tree- ferns, and disappeared behind the forest.
“A pterodactyl!” Challenger cried.
Summerlee gave a short laugh. “A large bird.”
Lord John had been watching through field glasses. “I cannot tell you what it was,”
he said, “but I can tell you I have never seen a bird shaped like that.”
The next day we crossed a ridge and saw the cliffs.
They were exactly as Maple White had drawn them: a vast red wall rising high
above the plain, with thick vegetation along the top. Near one section stood a
separate rocky tower with a tree growing on its summit.
Even Summerlee became quiet. “Well?” Challenger asked proudly.
“The cliffs exist,” Summerlee said. “That proves the cliffs exist. Nothing more.”
We spent several days searching for a way up. The main wall was almost vertical.
At one point we found the entrance of an old cave, but the passage was blocked.
We climbed surrounding hills and examined cracks and ledges. Nothing reached the
plateau.
Then Challenger noticed that the separate rock tower stood close to the main cliff.
If we could climb the tower and somehow cross the gap, we might reach the top.
The climb was difficult but possible. We carried a rope up and reached the tree that
grew on the tower. From there we could see the green edge of the plateau only a
short distance away - but between us and it was a deep chasm.
Lord John looked at the tree. “If we cut it down in the right direction, it could fall
across the gap.”
Novel THE LOST WORLD 25

pages.topic: crashed across the chasm with its upper branches landing on the plateau.
pages.text:
For hours we worked with axes. At last the tree began to move. It fell slowly, then
crashed across the chasm with its upper branches landing on the plateau.
We had a bridge.
Challenger insisted on going first. He sat astride the trunk and moved carefully
across.
When he reached the far side, he climbed onto the plateau and raised both arms.
Summerlee crossed next, carrying two rifles. I followed.
Lord John came last, walking with a balance and calm that I could hardly believe.
For the first time, all four of us stood inside Maple White Land.
The air was warm and still. Thick bushes grew near the cliff, while taller trees
formed a dark forest beyond. Strange calls came from somewhere in the distance.
Challenger’s face shone with triumph.
“Professor Summerlee,” he said, “we
can now begin the investigation you
demanded.” Summerlee adjusted his
glasses. “We can begin it. I have not yet
said how it will end.”
We moved about fifty meters into the
bushes.
Then we heard a terrible cracking sound
behind us. We ran back.
The tree bridge was gone. Far below, its
broken trunk lay at the foot of the cliff.
At first we thought it had slipped. Then a
face appeared on the opposite rock tower.
It was Gomez.
His calm expression had disappeared. He looked across the gap at Lord John with
open hatred.
“You are trapped now!” he shouted. Lord John stepped forward. “Why?”
26 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: Gomez laughed. “Think of Pedro Lopez. He was my brother. You killed him. I have
pages.text:
Gomez laughed. “Think of Pedro Lopez. He was my brother. You killed him. I have
waited years for this.”
So the past had followed us into the unknown.
Gomez had pushed the tree from the tower after we crossed. The four of us were
now on a plateau surrounded by cliffs, with no known road down.
“Your bones will stay up there,” Gomez called.
A moment later Lord John raised his rifle. Gomez disappeared behind the rock. We
heard shouting and then silence.
Below us, however, Zambo had remained loyal. He climbed the opposite tower as
soon as Gomez and the others were gone.
“Tell me what to do!” he shouted.
We used a thin rope to pull food and ammunition across the gap. Zambo promised
to stay below and help us in any way he could.
As night came, we camped near the cliff with only a small lantern. Behind us
stretched the unexplored forest of the plateau.
We had reached the lost world. And now we could not leave it.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 27

CHAPTER
Trapped in the Lost World
30 Novel THE LOST WORLD

Trapped in the Lost World
Our first task was simple: find water and a safe place to camp. We followed a small
stream into the forest and built a rough shelter in an open area surrounded by thorny
branches. Lord John called it “Fort Challenger”. Professor Challenger pretended to
dislike the joke, but I noticed that he did not suggest a different name.
The plateau was unlike any place I had ever seen. Some plants looked familiar,
while others seemed larger or older in form. Insects of brilliant colors moved
through the air. Every distant sound made us stop and listen.
We did not have to wait long for proof that Challenger had been right.
One morning we entered a broad glade and saw several enormous animals feeding
among the trees. They stood on powerful back legs, using shorter front legs to pull
down branches.
Their heads were small compared with their heavy bodies and long tails.
“Iguanodons,” Challenger whispered.
Even Summerlee forgot to argue. His face changed from doubt to amazement.
There were adults and young ones. For several minutes we watched them in
silence. “You were right,” Summerlee said at last.
Challenger looked almost disappointed. “Of course I was right.”
Their peace did not last. The next time we returned, one of the great plant-eaters
had been torn apart. Deep claw and tooth marks showed that a far more dangerous
animal lived nearby.
“A large carnivorous dinosaur,” Summerlee said. “Possibly an allosaurus,”
Challenger replied.
Lord John checked his rifle. “Call it what you like. I prefer not to meet it at close
range.” Another discovery was even more disturbing.
We heard a constant harsh crying from a rocky hollow and crawled forward to
investigate.
Below us lay a swampy basin filled with pterodactyls. Hundreds of them crowded
Novel THE LOST WORLD 31

pages.topic: around pools of green water. Young animals moved between leathery eggs, while
pages.text:
around pools of green water. Young animals moved between leathery eggs, while
large adults rested on rocks with folded wings.
For Challenger and Summerlee, it was a scientific treasure. They whispered
excitedly about wings, teeth, nesting behavior, and species. Lord John and I were
more interested in the animals’ sharp beaks and watchful eyes.
We tried to withdraw quietly, but one creature saw us. Its cry was answered by
others. In seconds the sky seemed full of wings.
“Run!” Lord John shouted.
We raced towards the trees. Beaks snapped
near our heads. Wings struck our shoulders.
One pterodactyl stabbed me in the neck
with its beak. Lord John’s coat was torn.
Challenger was knocked down. At last Lord
John fired his rifle and the attack weakened
enough for us to escape beneath thicker
branches.
Summerlee, bleeding from a cut on his
forehead, looked back toward the swamp.
“Remarkable,” he said.
“Remarkable?” Lord John replied. “They
nearly killed us.” “That does not make them
less remarkable.”
The scientists collected every fact they could, even when the facts had teeth.
When we returned to Fort Challenger, we found another problem. Something had
entered the camp while we were away. Food tins had been crushed. A wooden
ammunition box had been broken. Supplies were scattered across the ground.
There were no clear footprints. “Whatever did this was strong,” I said.
“And clever enough to enter without breaking the thorn wall,” Lord John added.
A large branch hung over one side of the camp. Something could have climbed
32 Novel THE LOST WORLD

through the tree.
That night we kept two fires burning and took turns on watch.
In the following days we explored carefully. We saw more iguanodons, giant
insects, strange birds, and tracks we could not identify. Once, at dusk, a huge
shadow moved between the trees. It was too large to be any modern animal I knew.
Despite the danger, Challenger was happier than I had ever seen him. The
plateau was proving his story in every direction. Summerlee, now convinced that
prehistoric life had survived, became just as energetic. Their arguments continued,
but the subject had changed. They no longer argued about whether the lost world
existed; they argued about how to classify everything inside it.
Lord John focused on survival. He chose safe paths, watched the wind, studied
animal tracks, and never allowed us to walk carelessly into thick cover.
I tried to do both jobs: observe and survive. I was a reporter, and I knew that if we
ever returned to London, people would want a clear record of what we had seen.
But returning was still the great question.
Every day we went to the cliff and called to Zambo. He remained at his little camp
below, faithful to his promise. Some of the Indigenous guides had gone back
toward the river, carrying letters from me and requests for strong rope. We could
only hope help would eventually arrive.
Meanwhile the plateau held another mystery.
More than once we had the feeling that we were being watched.
A shadow moved high in a tree and disappeared. We heard a clicking call unlike
any bird.
Food vanished from places we thought were secure. Once Lord John found a
footprint that looked disturbingly human, but broader and heavier.
“There may be people here,” I said.
“Or something close to people,” Challenger replied.
Summerlee frowned. “Let us not create a theory before we have evidence.” It was
Novel THE LOST WORLD 33

pages.topic: good advice. Yet the forest seemed to be giving us a warning.
pages.text:
good advice. Yet the forest seemed to be giving us a warning.
One afternoon I climbed a high tree at the edge of a clearing. From the upper
branches I hoped to see more of the plateau and perhaps discover a possible escape
route.
The view was astonishing.
The plateau was far larger than I had imagined. Forest covered most of it, but in the
center lay a broad lake shining in the sun. On the far side I could make out a line of
cliffs with dark openings that might be caves.
Then I noticed something else.
A thin line of smoke rose near those caves. Smoke meant fire.
And fire usually meant people.
I climbed down with my mind racing.
The lost world was not only a land of prehistoric animals. Someone - or something
- was living there too.
34 Novel THE LOST WORLD

CHAPTER
Malone’s Night Adventure
Novel THE LOST WORLD 37

Malone’s Night Adventure
My companions were pleased with what I had seen from the tree. That evening, by
the light of our fire, I drew a rough map of the plateau. We marked the cliff where
we had entered, the forest, the pterodactyl swamp, and the large lake in the center.
“The man who first saw the lake should name it,” Lord John said. I thought of
Gladys and the reason I had first wanted adventure. “Lake Gladys,” I said.
Summerlee gave me a dry look, but Challenger nodded. “Lake Gladys it is.”
I should have been satisfied with the day’s work. Instead, I became restless. I
wanted to prove that I could contribute more than notes and maps. I also wanted to
examine the signs of human life near the far side of the lake.
That night, after the others were asleep, I took a rifle, some food, and a small
electric lamp.
I left Fort Challenger alone.
At first the forest was peaceful. Moonlight appeared through gaps in the leaves.
I followed the stream, using the map in my head. The farther I traveled, the more
foolish my decision seemed, but pride kept me moving.
After several hours I reached the lake.
Its surface reflected the moon. For a few minutes I forgot the danger and simply
watched.
Then a heavy shape moved near the water.
An enormous stegosaurus stepped into the open.
I recognized it immediately from Maple White’s drawing. Plates rose along its back,
and spikes extended from its tail. It lowered its head to drink, completely unaware
of me.
I wanted to shout with excitement, but I remained still. This was living proof of a
world that should have disappeared millions of years ago.
Then the stegosaurus suddenly lifted its head. It had heard something.
38 Novel THE LOST WORLD

So had I.
A deep movement came from the bushes behind me. I turned and saw two shining
eyes.
The creature that stepped into the moonlight was built for killing. It stood on
powerful back legs with a long tail for balance. Its huge head was filled with teeth.
Whether it was an allosaurus or another great hunter, I did not care. It had seen me.
I ran.
Branches struck my face as I pushed
through the forest. Behind me I heard
heavy feet crashing closer. I fired once
over my shoulder. The shot did not stop
it.
The ground suddenly vanished.
I fell several meters into a deep pit and
landed painfully on soft earth.
For a moment I could not breathe. I
expected the dinosaur to fall after me,
but it stopped at the edge. Its head
appeared against the sky. It snapped its
jaws and roared, unable to reach me.
Eventually it moved away.
I examined the pit. Its sides were too straight to be natural. Sharp stakes had once
been placed at the bottom, though many were broken or rotten. This was a trap
made by intelligent hands.
The smoke I had seen from the tree had not been an accident. People really did live
on the plateau.
It took me a long time to climb out using roots and cracks in the wall. By dawn I
was exhausted, covered in mud, and far from camp.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 39

pages.topic: When I finally returned to Fort Challenger, something was wrong. The camp was
pages.text:
When I finally returned to Fort Challenger, something was wrong. The camp was
silent.
Challenger, Summerlee, and Lord John had disappeared.
There were signs of struggle. Equipment had been thrown aside. Some food was
missing.
On the ground I found broken branches and several broad footprints. I called until
my throat hurt. No one answered.
For the first time since we reached the plateau, I felt completely alone.
I spent the day searching nearby paths, but found no clear trail. At sunset I returned
to camp and prepared for a lonely night. I had almost fallen asleep when a hand
touched my arm.
I reached for my rifle - then stopped. Lord John Roxton knelt beside me.
He looked terrible. His clothes were torn, his face scratched, and he was breathing
hard.
“Quickly, Malone,” he whispered. “Take the rifles, cartridges, and some food. We
cannot stay here.”
I followed him into thick bushes where he had chosen a hiding place. “Where are
the professors?” I asked.
“Captured.” “By whom?”
Lord John’s face became hard. “Ape-men.”
He told me what had happened. Before dawn, while the others were waking, large
creatures dropped from the branches above the camp. They were covered with
reddish hair, but they walked upright. They carried clubs and stones, communicated
with one another, and used strong vines to tie their prisoners.
Lord John had fired at them, but they attacked too quickly. The three men were
overwhelmed.
“They are stronger than ordinary men,” he said. “And they are clever. Not human
as we are, but not simply animals either.”
40 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: The ape-men had carried Challenger, Summerlee, and Lord John through the forest.
pages.text:
The ape-men had carried Challenger, Summerlee, and Lord John through the forest.
Their leader was a powerful older creature.
Then Lord John gave a tired smile.
“You will not believe this part. The chief looks like Challenger. Same broad
shoulders, same beard, same angry expression. Even Summerlee laughed when he
saw them together.”
The strange similarity may have saved Challenger. The ape-men treated him
differently, almost as if they considered him important. Summerlee and Lord John
were handled far more roughly.
During the confusion, Lord John managed to escape. He had returned to find me
and collect weapons.
“Can we rescue them?” I asked.
“We must try. But there is more. The ape-men have other prisoners - humans from
another part of the plateau. I saw several of them being dragged towards the ape
settlement.”
He checked his rifle.
“If we move carefully, we may reach them before it is too late.”
I looked at the dark forest. Only a few hours earlier I had been proud of my solo
journey. Now it seemed childish. Courage was not wandering into danger to prove
something about yourself.
Real courage was going back into danger because other people needed you. “Lead
the way,” I said.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 41

CHAPTER
Prisoners of the Ape-Men
44 Novel THE LOST WORLD

Prisoners of the Ape-Men
Lord John and I moved slowly through the forest. We avoided open ground and
stopped whenever we heard the strange clicking calls of the ape-men. More than
once we hid in bushes while a group passed close by.
Near the cliff we could see Zambo far below, still waiting at his camp. I wanted to
call to him, but Lord John shook his head. A shout could reveal our position.
After two hours he raised one hand and pointed ahead.
Through the leaves I saw a large clearing. Huts made from branches had been
built high in the surrounding trees. Ape-men crowded the branches and the ground
below. In the center stood several prisoners.
I recognized Professor Summerlee at once. His clothes were torn and his head was
bowed.
Challenger stood nearby, guarded but not tied as tightly. Beside them were several
small, strong-looking human prisoners - members of the group whose smoke I had
seen near the lake.
Lord John pulled me back into cover.
“We wait until we have a clear shot,” he whispered. What happened next was
difficult to watch.
The ape-men led one of the human prisoners to the edge of the cliff. Far below,
sharp bamboo canes grew from the ground. The prisoners were being forced over
the edge as part of a cruel ceremony.
One man was thrown.
The ape-men shouted and jumped with excitement. Summerlee was brought
forward next.
Challenger struggled against his guards. He shouted and tried to stop them, but the
Novel THE LOST WORLD 45

ape chief pushed him aside.
Lord John raised his rifle. “Now,” he said.
His first shot hit the chief. The creature fell.
I fired at the guards holding Summerlee. Lord John fired again. Confusion spread
through the clearing. The ape-men had never faced rifles at close range. They did
not understand where the sudden attack was coming from.
“Move!” Lord John shouted.
Challenger seized Summerlee and pulled him towards the trees. I ran out to meet
them and pushed a loaded rifle into Challenger’s hands. Lord John covered our
retreat.
The remaining human prisoners followed us. Ape-men rushed from the bushes
behind, but each time they came too close,
Lord John’s accurate shooting forced them
back.
Summerlee was exhausted and could barely
walk. Challenger and I supported him
between us.
After a long, desperate retreat, we reached
our hidden shelter in the thick bushes.
For several minutes no one spoke.
Then Summerlee looked at me. “Mr
Malone,” he said weakly, “I believe I owe
you and Lord John a considerable debt.”
“You can repay it by staying alive,” Lord John replied.
The rescued prisoners called themselves Accala. We could not understand their
language, but one young man was clearly their leader. He had a shaved area at the
46 Novel THE LOST WORLD

front of his head and carried himself with quiet authority. The others treated him
with great respect.
Using gestures, he explained that the Accala lived in caves on the far side of Lake
Gladys. The ape-men controlled the forest on this side of the plateau. The two
groups had fought for generations. The ape-men often captured Accala hunters and
carried them away.
The young chief repeatedly pointed towards the lake, then at us, then toward the
forest of the ape-men. He wanted to return to his people.
“We should go with them,” Challenger said. “Their caves may reveal how humans
first reached the plateau.”
Summerlee looked at him in disbelief. “Our first task is to escape this place.”
“And how do you propose to do that without learning more about its inhabitants?”
For once, Lord John ended the argument quickly. “The ape-men know our old
camp. We cannot stay here. The Accala have friends, food, and a defensible
position. We go with them.”
The next afternoon we started across the plateau.
We were a strange group: four exhausted travelers carrying modern rifles, several
rescued Accala, and a young chief guiding us through a land of dinosaurs.
At the shore of Lake Gladys, the Accala suddenly began shouting with joy. A fleet
of canoes was moving across the water towards us.
The young chief’s people had come looking for him.
When the canoes reached shore, dozens of Accala rushed forward. They embraced
the rescued men and surrounded their young leader. Many then turned toward us
and bowed or touched our hands. It was clear that they understood we had helped
save him.
We crossed the lake in their canoes. For the first time I saw the far cliffs closely.
Many dark cave entrances opened high above the ground, reached by narrow stone
steps.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 47

pages.topic: showed iguanodons, flying reptiles, huge fish-like animals, and many shapes we
pages.text:
The Accala village was protected from large animals by its height. Inside the caves
were sleeping areas, stores, tools, and drawings of the plateau’s creatures. The walls
showed iguanodons, flying reptiles, huge fish-like animals, and many shapes we
had not yet seen.
Challenger and Summerlee forgot their
exhaustion. They examined everything. “A
natural record of the animal life,” Summerlee
said.
“And perhaps of its history,” Challenger added.
That evening the Accala held a council. The
young chief spoke passionately, pointing again
and again toward the forest of the ape-men. We
could not follow his words, but we understood
the meaning.
He wanted to fight.
Lord John watched him carefully. “He thinks
this is his chance. Their enemies have captured and killed his people for years.
Now he has us and our rifles.”
Summerlee frowned. “We did not come here to join a war.”
“No,” Lord John said, “but the ape-men will come after us anyway. And these
people saved us by giving us shelter.”
Challenger nodded. “If their victory also gives us safe access to the plateau, it may
be necessary.”
I thought of the prisoners at the cliff. I did not want more violence, but I knew the
ape-men were already hunting us.
The next morning, hundreds of Accala gathered with spears and bows. The four of
us checked our rifles.
The expedition had come to search for scientific truth.
Now we were about to take part in a battle for the lost world.
48 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: Was it the safest option available? Explain.

pages.text:
CHAPTER
The Battle for the Plateau
Novel THE LOST WORLD 51

The Battle for the Plateau
The Accala force moved towards the forest in a long line. Scouts went ahead, while
the main group followed with bows and spears. Lord John and Summerlee took the
right side. Challenger and I moved on the left.
No one spoke much. Even Challenger seemed to understand that this was not a
scientific demonstration.
The first attack came suddenly.
A group of ape-men rushed from the trees, swinging heavy clubs and throwing
stones. The Accala were faster. They moved aside, fired arrows and spears, and
surrounded the attackers before they could break the line.
The battle became more dangerous inside the forest.
Ape-men dropped from branches. Others charged from behind bushes. Their
strength was enormous. One blow broke Summerlee’s rifle. An Accala warrior
pulled him away before another strike could reach him.
Our rifles gave the Accala an important advantage, but we used them only when the
fighting came close. Lord John moved calmly from one position to another, never
wasting a shot.
After more than an hour, the ape-men began to retreat. The Accala followed.
We reached their tree settlement later that day. The fighting there was fierce but
short. The power of the ape-men was broken, and their organized resistance ended.
Many were killed during the battle and pursuit. The surviving females and young
were taken under Accala control. It was a harsh ending to a conflict that had lasted
for generations, and I found little joy in it.
Challenger, however, viewed the event as a turning point in the history of the
plateau.
Summerlee had a simpler response.
52 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: - and then, if possible, to London.”
pages.text:
“I have seen enough battles for one lifetime,” he said. “Now let us return to science
- and then, if possible, to London.”
The victory changed our position completely. The Accala now treated us as honored
allies. We could travel more safely through much of the plateau, and they invited us
to stay in their caves.
We chose to camp nearby instead. Lord John did not want to depend completely on
people whose language we still could not understand.
For the next several days our attention returned to exploration.
At Lake Gladys we saw creatures with long
necks and powerful swimming bodies.
Challenger and Summerlee agreed that they
resembled plesiosaurs, marine reptiles known
from fossils. Seeing them alive in fresh water
was almost impossible to accept, even after
everything else we had witnessed.
We also learned that the Accala treated some
iguanodons like herds of cattle. Marks on the
animals showed different owners. The huge
plant-eaters could be guided and controlled far
more easily than their size suggested.
But the plateau still contained predators that no one could control.
One afternoon people began racing toward the caves. A warning cry spread through
the camp. Two enormous meat-eating dinosaurs burst from the edge of the forest,
chasing a group of hunters.
They moved with frightening speed.
Lord John and I fired. One turned toward us, and for a moment I saw its open jaws
and powerful legs coming directly across the grass. More shots followed. The
Novel THE LOST WORLD 53

pages.topic: creature fell only a short distance away.
pages.text:
creature fell only a short distance away.
The Accala did not treat the event as unusual. To them, the dinosaurs were part of
daily life. For us, every new creature expanded the list of discoveries we hoped to
carry home.
Summerlee collected insects and plants. Challenger made notes about reptiles and
geology. Lord John preserved the skull of a huge flightless predatory bird called
a Phorusrhacos after we encountered one near the lake. We also observed a large,
heavy plant-eating mammal about the size of a rhinoceros, which the professors
identified as a toxodon.
Yet our scientific success made the problem of escape more urgent. We had
evidence that could change what people understood about natural history. If we
died on the plateau, most of that knowledge would disappear with us.
We asked the Accala how they had reached the plateau. Through signs and
drawings, they showed us that an old passage had once connected the cliffs with the
land below. An earthquake had blocked the upper part about a year earlier.
That explained why Maple White and perhaps others had been able to enter in the
past. “So there was a road,” I said.
“There was,” Summerlee replied. “That is not the same as saying there is one now.”
The Accala were surprisingly unwilling to help us leave. At first we thought they
did not understand. Then the reason became clearer. They believed our weapons
had brought them victory. They wanted us to stay as protectors.
Whenever we asked for long ropes, strong leather strips, or timber for an escape
bridge, they smiled and refused.
Only the young chief we had rescued - whose name sounded to us like Maretas -
showed sympathy. He watched our failed attempts and seemed troubled.
Meanwhile we continued to communicate with Zambo below the original cliff
whenever we could reach that side of the plateau. He had not abandoned us.
“Help will come,” he called up. “I stay here!”
54 Novel THE LOST WORLD

His loyalty gave us hope, but a rescue party could do little if we had no safe way
down from the top.
One evening Challenger announced that he had a plan.
“I require several days,” he said, “and I require that none of you interfere.”
Summerlee sighed. “That sentence has never led to anything peaceful.” Challenger
only smiled.
At almost the same time, Lord John began making private journeys towards the
pterodactyl swamp. He built a light cage from bent canes and carried it around
himself as protection from attacking beaks.
“What are you doing there?” I asked. “Studying,” he said.
“Studying what?”
“You will find out when I am ready.”
So, while the professors searched for knowledge, Lord John followed a secret of his
own, and Challenger worked on an even stranger idea.
We had survived dinosaurs, betrayal, captivity, and battle. Our final enemy was the
cliff itself.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 55

CHAPTER
The Hidden Way Home
58 Novel THE LOST WORLD

The Hidden Way Home
Professor Challenger eventually led us to a small clearing
where hot gas bubbled through a mud pool. Around it he
had arranged bamboo tubes, leather straps, and a huge
dried membrane made from part of a prehistoric animal.
Summerlee stopped in disbelief. “What is that?”
“Our way down,” Challenger said.
The gas from the ground, he explained, contained
hydrogen. He had collected it inside the large membrane
to create a balloon. If the balloon could lift one person at
a time, perhaps we could descend from the plateau.
Lord John was delighted by the idea. Summerlee called it
madness.
Challenger attached a heavy stone to the balloon to test
its lifting power. The experiment worked far too well.
The balloon shot upwards, pulled Challenger off his feet,
and almost carried him into the air. I grabbed Challenger,
Lord John grabbed me, and for one ridiculous second all
of us were being dragged across the ground together.
Then the rope snapped.
The balloon and stone disappeared into the sky.
Challenger stood up, brushed dirt from his clothes, and
looked pleased. “An excellent demonstration,” he said.
Summerlee stared at him. “You nearly killed us.”
“A small technical problem. The principle is proved.”
He promised to build another balloon, but none of us felt
completely confident about becoming its passenger.
During these same days I traveled twice to the original
cliff to speak with Zambo. He told me that one of our
Novel THE LOST WORLD 59

messengers had gone to search for stronger ropes and more men. Help should arrive
soon.
On my second return journey I met Lord John near the pterodactyl swamp. He was
inside his strange cane cage.
“Still studying?” I asked.
“Very seriously,” he said with a smile. He would tell me no more.
When I reached the Accala camp, I noticed that Maretas was waiting for me.
He looked around to make sure no one was watching, then touched my arm and
pointed towards one of the caves.
I followed him.
He led me up a narrow stair and into a passage deeper than the others. At the back
wall he moved several stones and revealed a small opening.
Then he pointed at me, at the opening, and finally downwards. My heart began to
beat faster.
“A way out?” I asked, though he could not understand the words. Maretas nodded.
That night I brought Challenger, Summerlee, and Lord John to the place. We
carried lamps and rope. Maretas was gone, perhaps to avoid being seen helping us.
The hidden passage was narrow at first, then widened. We moved through darkness
for hundreds of meters. At one point part of the tunnel had collapsed, and we had to
crawl over loose rock. Beyond it we found a larger natural cave.
Ahead, a red glow seemed to block the passage. We hurried towards it.
“The moon!” Lord John cried.
A round opening in the cliff showed the full moon outside. We had found a second
exit from the plateau.
The opening was too small to have been noticed easily from below, and the cliff
curved over it. We tested the distance to the ground. With our rope, the descent
would be possible.
Summerlee sat down on a rock and laughed with relief.
60 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: “At last,” he said. “A plan that does not involve flying inside a dinosaur.”
pages.text:
“At last,” he said. “A plan that does not involve flying inside a dinosaur.”
We returned quietly to camp. The next day we prepared to leave without telling the
Accala leaders. They had treated us generously, but we were no longer sure they
would allow us to go.
We took only what we could carry: rifles, ammunition, notebooks, a few specimens,
and essential supplies. Challenger insisted on bringing one large wooden case.
“What is inside?” Summerlee asked. “Scientific material.”
“That answer usually means trouble.” Challenger refused to explain.
After dark we climbed to the hidden passage. Before entering, I looked back across
the plateau.
Small fires shone near the Accala caves. Beyond them stretched the forest. Lake
Gladys reflected the moon. Somewhere in the distance an unknown animal gave a
long cry.
I had dreamed of adventure in London, but I had never imagined anything like
this place. We had been frightened, injured, trapped, and sometimes divided by
argument. Yet the lost world had also changed us. We had learned to depend on one
another.
We entered the cave.
Two hours later we reached the opening in the
outer cliff. Lord John went first, using the rope. I
followed, then Summerlee. Challenger came last,
still protecting his heavy case.
When my feet touched the ground below, I wanted
to shout. I had not realized how strongly I had
missed ordinary earth.
We made our way through the night towards
Zambo’s camp. At dawn we saw smoke ahead -
not one fire, but many.
A rescue party had arrived with twenty men,
ropes, and equipment. Zambo ran towards us with a smile so wide that it seemed to
light his whole face.
Novel THE LOST WORLD 61

pages.topic: “You come back! I knew you would come back!”
pages.text:
“You come back! I knew you would come back!”
For the first time in weeks, we were truly safe.
The return journey to the Amazon was long, but it felt simple after the plateau. We
traveled downriver, reached Para, and finally sailed for England.
Challenger guarded his wooden case as if it contained the future of science. Lord
John also protected a small box that he refused to discuss.
Summerlee organized his insect and plant specimens. I wrote as much of our story
as I could remember.
There was one thing I still thought about often: Gladys.
I had left England hoping to become the kind of man she might admire. I was
returning after facing more danger than either of us could have imagined.
I wondered what she would say when she saw me again.
62 Novel THE LOST WORLD

CHAPTER
Proof Before the World
Novel THE LOST WORLD 65

Proof Before the World
London welcomed us as if we had returned from another planet. Newspapers
printed rumors about the expedition, but many scientists still doubted our
story. Damaged photographs, drawings, unusual insects, and bones could all be
questioned.
A special meeting was arranged at the Zoological Institute.
The hall was even more crowded than the one where our journey had begun.
Professor Summerlee gave the main report. He described our route without
revealing the exact location of the plateau. Then he spoke about the animals we had
seen: iguanodons, stegosaurs, pterodactyls, giant predators, strange birds, enormous
reptiles in the lake, and many new species of insects and plants.
This time Summerlee was not the skeptic. He was a witness. Yet some members of
the audience remained unconvinced.
One scientist stood and argued that photographs could be altered, specimens could
come from other places, and even honest travelers could make mistakes.
The hall filled with angry voices. Challenger rose slowly.
“What evidence would satisfy you?” he asked. “The animal itself,” the sceptic
replied.
Challenger smiled. I knew that smile.
He signaled to me. With Zambo’s help, I brought the heavy wooden case from
behind the platform. The same case Challenger had protected during our escape
now stood in front of hundreds of people.
The room became silent. Challenger opened the lid.
For a moment nothing happened. Then a leathery head appeared.
A living pterodactyl climbed onto the edge of the box.
The audience froze. Some people screamed. Others stood on chairs to see. The
66 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: animal spread its wings, beat the air, and rose above the platform.
pages.text:
animal spread its wings, beat the air, and rose above the platform.
It circled the hall once.
Then it flew towards an open window and disappeared into the London night. No
one laughed at Professor Challenger after that.
Our story was proved in the most dramatic way possible.
There was one private matter I had to face after the meeting. I went to Gladys’s
house expecting - I am embarrassed to admit - a scene of admiration and happiness.
She was surprised to see me. “Edward! You are back.” “Yes.”
Something in the room felt different. Then a small man stood from an armchair.
Gladys looked uncomfortable. “Edward, this is my husband, William Potts.”
For several seconds I could say nothing.
She had written to me while I was away,
but the letter had never reached me. “I
thought you wanted a man of adventure,”
I said at last.
Gladys gave a small, uncertain smile.
“Perhaps I learned that I wanted a quieter
life.”
William Potts was not an explorer. He
was not famous. He had never crossed
the Amazon or faced a dinosaur. He was
simply the man she had chosen.
I left feeling foolish and hurt.
During the following week, however, my disappointment became less painful. I
began to understand something important. I had started the expedition because I
wanted to prove myself to Gladys. But the journey had become much larger than
Novel THE LOST WORLD 67

pages.topic: no newspaper reporter had ever expected to see.
pages.text:
that. I had faced danger for my friends, worked as part of a team, and seen things
no newspaper reporter had ever expected to see.
My life no longer needed Gladys’s approval to have value.
A few evenings later, the four explorers met again in Lord John’s rooms. After
dinner he placed an old box on the table.
“I have one final surprise,” he said.
He poured out a group of rough stones. Challenger and Summerlee looked puzzled.
“Remember the blue clay in the pterodactyl swamp?” Lord John asked. “I have
seen blue volcanic clay like that before - in a diamond mine. That is why I kept
going back.”
He had collected the stones secretly and had one tested after our return. It was a
valuable diamond.
“The whole group is worth at least two hundred thousand pounds,” he said. “Four
equal shares.”
For once, even Challenger had no immediate reply.
Lord John turned to him. “What will you do with your share?”
“Build a private museum,” Challenger said. “A proper home for scientific
research.” Summerlee smiled. “I will retire from teaching and finish work I have
postponed for years.”
Lord John nodded. “I intend to organize another expedition to the plateau. Better
prepared this time.”
Then he looked at me. “And you, Malone? I suppose you will marry and settle
down.”
I thought of Gladys, then of the red cliffs, the moon over the lake, the dark forest,
and the thrill of stepping into the unknown.
“Not yet,” I said. “If you will take me, I would rather go with you.” Lord John
68 Novel THE LOST WORLD

pages.topic: reached across the table and shook my hand.
pages.text:
reached across the table and shook my hand.
So my first great adventure ended with the promise of another.
When I had asked Gladys what kind of man she could admire, I believed courage
was something a person could win like a prize. The lost world taught me otherwise.
Courage is a choice made again and again - when the road is uncertain, when fear is
real, and when someone else is depending on you.
I had gone to South America hoping to become a hero.
I came home understanding that adventure was not about looking heroic.
It was about discovering what you were capable of when the world became larger
than your plans.
The End
